rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage warns that opponents have razed monotheism and sympathy, wrecked social order, and made themselves deserving of divine punishment.
rows.anchor: They are guilty of razing to ground the two foundations of the religion of nature: monotheism and sympathy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage promises Muslims divine aid and dominance, showing through cosmic signs that God can turn adverse circumstances favorable when He wills mercy.
rows.anchor: when God wants to shower His mercy on someone He transforms unfavourable circumstances into favourable ones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and his companions are urged to remain with the religion of human nature and disregard those who have become blind and deaf.
rows.anchor: fully adhere to the religion of nature and are told to ignore all those who have become blind and deaf.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier verses rebutted Quraysh's doubts about Muslim ascendancy, monotheism, and the hereafter; they had drawn those doubts from Persia's victory.
rows.anchor: They had raised these doubts by using the victory of the Persians in their favour.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse preludes a warning: Quraysh must face the consequences of their disorder rather than trust childish assurances, since their deities cannot rescue them.
rows.anchor: They should not try to satisfy themselves on the basis of these childish assurances and in fact face the reality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone creates, provides, controls death, and resurrects; Quraysh cannot claim their deities perform or assist in any of these acts, so they cannot rely on them if God seizes them.
rows.anchor: They cannot claim that a single one of these tasks are done by their deities or they help God in them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shifts from direct address to Quraysh in its first part to indirect address in its final phrase; Islahi points to explanations of this eloquence elsewhere in his exegesis.
rows.anchor: the first part of the verse was addressed directly to the Quraysh, the last part

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like paired expressions such as day and night, “land and sea” comprehensively includes every sphere of life, individual or collective and ideological or practical.
rows.anchor: the expression land and sea

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sound ideology depends on faith in God and firm practice on Islam; they require each other, so the loss of either entails the other's collapse and the loss of both brings disorder everywhere.
rows.anchor: The correctness in view and ideology is entirely based on faith in God and the resoluteness of practice is based on Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Any apparent vitality after both foundations are destroyed is only temporary, and people who prize it are deceiving themselves.
rows.anchor: if, in spite of the razing down of the two, there seems some spark of life anywhere, then it is just transient.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about making people taste some consequences of their deeds describes God answering their misdeeds and aims to make them heed the warning and return from wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: The purpose is to induce them to pay heed and return to the right path by abandoning their ill-ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messenger nations face a warning torment meant to jolt them and a later torment meant to vanquish them; Quraysh is warned of the first, followed by the crushing second if they do not reform.
rows.anchor: the nations of God’s messengers face two types of torments: first, to jolt them and second to finally vanquish them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to direct Quraysh to inspect the remains and fate of earlier peoples, most of whom were polytheists like them.
rows.anchor: they should observe the fate of the previous nations by looking at their remnants. Most of these people were polytheists like them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only a few among Quraysh and earlier peoples worshipped God purely; God sifted out those few and destroyed the rest.
rows.anchor: among these previous nations too very few purely worshipped God. Finally, God sifted out these few people and destroyed the rest.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address turns to the Prophet and companions, as at 30:31: if the stubborn opponents will not listen, believers should ignore them, focus on God's natural religion, and prepare for the inevitable Judgment.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) and his companions are addressed the way they are in verse 31 earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On Judgment Day people separate and cannot benefit one another; their present reliance on deities, intercessors, or clan will fail, echoing 30:14's “yatafarraqūn.”
rows.anchor: on that day every one will be separated from one another; no one will be of any benefit to anyone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each person bears the outcome of their own deeds: disbelievers face their disbelief alone, while the righteous prepare their own future and alone receive its reward.
rows.anchor: everyone will be rewarded or punished according to his deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 45 connects to the promised Day in verse 43: the Hereafter's real aim is to reward believers by grace, while punishment of disbelievers is only a necessary consequence.
rows.anchor: the real objective of the Hereafter is to reward the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers' reward is granted through God's grace, not merely as payment for their deeds, and human measures cannot comprehend its extent.
rows.anchor: the reward given to the believers will not merely be because of their good deeds but in accordance with the grace of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God does not love disbelievers conveys abhorrence; Islahi says their resulting abode is Hell and God does not care about them.
rows.anchor: Words are unable to express the abhorrence found in the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wind signs assure the Prophet and Muslims that, as God brings mercy and sustenance to suffocating conditions through favorable winds, He will create favorable circumstances for them.
rows.anchor: the Almighty sends favourable winds to suffocating environments which come as glad tidings of mercy to people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Favorable winds let ships sail at God's command, enabling travel from place to place.
rows.anchor: it is these favourable winds because of which ships sail at the behest of God so that people can travel from one place to another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Seeking God's bounty” means seeking God's sustenance through trade.
rows.anchor: so that people seek God’s sustenance through trade

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The providential system is set up so people can benefit from God's favors and express gratitude.
rows.anchor: all this system of providence has been set up so that people can benefit from God’s favours and express gratitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's aid and blessings for Muslims entail gratitude; after receiving them, they must not become indifferent to Him.
rows.anchor: after receiving them they must not become indifferent to God; on the contrary, these favours entail that they must remain grateful to Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Historical precedent explains the preceding assurance: Muhammad is not the first messenger, and God's established practice with earlier messengers will also apply in his case.
rows.anchor: The way His established practice manifested itself for them, it will also manifest itself in his case.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier messengers brought clear proofs, but their nations became hostile to believers and their companions; God punished those nations for that wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: Finally, as a consequence of this wrong attitude towards the believers, God punished them.
